actual_current_steps.1.1: For every Schwartz component $f$ and every integer $N$, the finite expansion of $\prod_{j=1}^3(1+|x_j|)^N$ is controlled term-by-term by the seminorms in [F1], so $|f(x)|\le C_N\prod_j(1+|x_j|)^{-N}$; the same holds for its derivatives. Choose $N=4$. Each component of each vector integrand defining $J_{\mathrm{kin}}$, $L_{\mathrm{can}}$, and $S_{\mathrm{can}}$ is a sum of products of two Schwartz components, with at most one coordinate factor. Therefore, for each such vector integrand $V$, $\sum_{j=1}^3|V_j(x)|\le C_VG(x)$ for some $C_V\ge0$, where $G(x):=\prod_{j=1}^3(1+|x_j|)^{-7}$. By [F5], for $R>0$ the one-dimensional factor satisfies $\int_{-R}^{R}(1+|s|)^{-7}\,ds=\frac13(1-(1+R)^{-6})\le\frac13$ and tends to $1/3$. Riemann-Fubini [F4] gives $\int_{Q_R}G\,d^3x=\left(\frac13(1-(1+R)^{-6})\right)^3\le1/27$. Thus the nonnegative cube integrals $A_R(V):=\int_{Q_R}\sum_{j=1}^3|V_j(x)|\,d^3x$ are bounded above by $C_V/27$ and are nondecreasing in $R$ by finite-slice additivity and monotonicity [F6]. The set $\{A_R(V):R>0\}$ is nonempty (take $R=1$) and bounded above, so its finite real supremum $A(V)$ exists by [F7]. For every $\varepsilon>0$, choose $R_0$ with $A_{R_0}(V)>A(V)-\varepsilon$; then $A(V)-\varepsilon<A_R(V)\le A(V)$ for all $R\ge R_0$, proving that $A_R(V)$ has a finite limit. Hence each $V$ is absolutely integrable in the preceding Definition's sense, and its signed component integrals have finite cube-exhaustion limits by the proved absolute-tail implication in [F1]. This proves that all three functionals are well-defined finite vectors. [given, F1, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

actual_current_steps.3.1:
For $\psi\in D(H_\epsilon)$, differentiate
$ F(s)\psi:=U_\epsilon(s)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a_s)U_\epsilon(s)\psi . $
The domain preservation in [F4] and step 1.2 justify the product rule in $L^2$; the symbol derivative in step 2.1 is also an operator-norm derivative by [F6], since the symbols and their difference quotients have common compact support and converge with all derivatives required by that estimate. The two Hamiltonian terms combine to $U_\epsilon(s)^*(i/\epsilon)[H_\epsilon,\operatorname{Op}(a_s)]U_\epsilon(s)$; $\partial_s\operatorname{Op}(a_s)=-\operatorname{Op}(\{a_s,h\})$ cancels its Poisson term by step 1.2. Therefore
$ F'(s)\psi=\epsilon^2U_\epsilon(s)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a_s,V})U_\epsilon(s)\psi . $
Step 2.1 gives a uniform bound on $p_{12d+16}(a_s)$. The remainder estimate [F5] followed by [F6] consequently yields
$ \sup_{|s|,|t|\le T}\|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a_s,V})\|\le C_{T,V,a}. $
The derivative must also be continuous up to the endpoints to use [F7]. The local remainder formula in [[lem-nrqmx-cubic-moyal-commutator-remainder]] is linear in its symbol argument. For fixed $t$, the symbols $a_s$ have common compact support on the interval and vary continuously in every Schwartz seminorm by step 2.1; applying the remainder estimate to $a_s-a_{s'}$ and then [F6] shows $\|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a_s,V})-\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a_{s'},V})\|\to0$ as $s'\to s$. Thus the remainder operators are norm-continuous. Strong continuity of $U_\epsilon(s)$ and its adjoint, together with uniform boundedness of these operators, makes $s\mapsto U_\epsilon(s)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a_s,V})U_\epsilon(s)\psi$ continuous for each fixed $\psi$. The derivative in the displayed formula therefore extends continuously to both endpoints. Integrate it by [F7], use unitarity, and evaluate the endpoints $F(t)\psi=U_\epsilon(t)^*\operatorname{Op}(a)U_\epsilon(t)\psi$ and $F(0)\psi=\operatorname{Op}(a\circ\Phi_t)\psi$. This gives the required $C_{T,V,a}|t|\epsilon^2\|\psi\|$ bound on the dense domain; boundedness of both endpoint operators extends it to all of $L^2$, uniformly for $|t|\le T$. Reversing the integration orientation gives the same estimate for $t<0$. [step 2.1, step 1.2, A2, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

The explicit collar is $(q,t)\mapsto(1-t)q$, where $q=e^{i\theta}\in S^1$ and $t=1-r\geq0$ is inward radial distance. Since $dx\wedge dy=r\,d\theta\wedge dt$, the induced boundary orientation at $t=0$ is increasing $\theta$ (counterclockwise). Define $h(s)=e^{-1/s}$ for $s>0$ and $h(s)=0$ for $s\leq0$. For $0\leq t\leq\epsilon/2$ set $\chi_0(t)=h(t)/(h(t)+h(\epsilon/2-t))$, and for $t\geq\epsilon/2$ set $\chi_0(t)=1$. Every derivative of $h$ vanishes at $0$, so $\chi_0$ is smooth, flat at $0$, positive for $t>0$, at most $1$, and equal to $1$ near $\epsilon$; hence $\int_0^\epsilon\chi_0(t)\,dt<\epsilon$. Put $b(t)=h(t-\epsilon/4)h(3\epsilon/4-t)$, a nonnegative smooth function supported in $[\epsilon/4,3\epsilon/4]$ with positive integral, and define $\chi=\chi_0+c b$ where $c=(\epsilon-\int_0^\epsilon\chi_0)/\int_0^\epsilon b>0$. Then $\chi$ is positive for $t>0$, flat at $0$, equals $1$ near $\epsilon$, and has integral $\epsilon$. Set $\rho(t)=\int_0^t\chi(s)\,ds$. Thus $\rho(0)=\rho'(0)=\rho''(0)=0$, $\rho'(t)>0$ for $t>0$, and $\rho(t)=t$ near $\epsilon$. Replace $f_j(q,t)$ by $f_j(q,\rho(t))$ in each collar. This preserves area integral: the pullback coefficient is multiplied by $\rho'(t)$, and substitution $s=\rho(t)$ gives the original integral. Now form $X=D_0^2\cup_{S^1}(-D_1^2)$ by gluing the standard boundary circles with the identity; the first disk has orientation $dx\wedge dy$, the second has its negative, and their induced boundary orientations are opposite. Use the signed collar coordinates $s=t$ on the first disk and $s=-t$ on the second as seam charts; together with the two disk interiors they define the smooth structure on $X$. Both sides have orientation $d\theta\wedge ds$. The modified maps have the same boundary trace and all normal derivatives through order two vanish at the seam, while their tangential derivatives through order two agree there. They therefore glue to a $C^2$ map $g:X\to S^2$. The double is compact, smooth and boundaryless, and its chosen orientation gives $\int_Xg^*\omega=\int_{D^2}f_0^*\omega-\int_{D^2}f_1^*\omega$. actual_current_steps.3.1: The inverse of $I+A$ is the bounded diagonal operator $B e_n=(n+1)^{-1}e_n$. Indeed for any $x\in\ell^2$, $y_n=x_n/(n+1)$ satisfies $\sum n^2|y_n|^2\le\sum|x_n|^2$, and $(I+A)y=x$. The operator $B$ is positive and injective, but it is not bounded below because $\|Be_n\|=(n+1)^{-1}\to0$ for unit vectors $e_n$. The vector $y=(1/n)_{n\ge1}$ belongs to $\ell^2$: for $n\ge2$, $n^{-2}\le(n-1)^{-1}-n^{-1}$, so $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}\le2$. It is not in $\operatorname{Ran}B$, since $Bx=y$ would require $x_n=(n+1)/n>1$ for every $n$, which is not square-summable. Hence $B$ is not surjective and $0\in\sigma(B)$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]
actual_current_steps.4.1: Define $E_B(S)x=\sum_{n:(n+1)^{-1}\in S}x_ne_n$ for Borel $S\subseteq\sigma(B)$. Its values are orthogonal coordinate projections, and the coordinate definition gives $E_B(\varnothing)=0$, $E_B(\sigma(B))=I$, and $E_B(S)E_B(T)=E_B(S\cap T)$. For disjoint Borel $S_k$, each coordinate $n$ occurs in at most one projection, so the partial sums $\sum_{k\le N}E_B(S_k)x$ converge in $\ell^2$ to $E_B(\bigcup_kS_k)x$: the squared norm of the omitted coordinates is a tail of the convergent nonnegative series $\sum_n|x_n|^2$. Thus $E_B$ is strongly countably additive. It integrates the coordinate function to $B$, because its integral acts diagonally by $(n+1)^{-1}$ on each $e_n$. For every $x$, its finite scalar measure is $\mu_x(S):=\langle E_B(S)x,x\rangle=\sum_{n:(n+1)^{-1}\in S}|x_n|^2$. For any Borel $S\subseteq\sigma(B)$, the finite set $K_N:=\{(n+1)^{-1}:n\le N,\ (n+1)^{-1}\in S\}$ is compact and contained in $S$, and $\mu_x(K_N)\uparrow\mu_x(S)$ because $\sum_n|x_n|^2<\infty$. Hence $\mu_x$ is inner regular on every Borel set. Since $\sigma(B)$ is compact, for any Borel $S$ and $\varepsilon>0$, inner regularity of $S^c$ gives a compact $K\subseteq S^c$ with $\mu_x(S^c\setminus K)<\varepsilon$; then the open set $\sigma(B)\setminus K$ contains $S$ and its excess measure is less than $\varepsilon$. Thus $\mu_x$ is also outer regular, so $E_B$ is a regular PVM. Hence [F1] identifies it with the bounded-resolvent spectral PVM. Since no atom is at zero, $E_B(\{0\})=0$, although step 3.1 proves $0\in\sigma(B)$. This refutes the asserted implication and shows why a zero spectral projection must be distinguished from a spectral value. [A1, F1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

Set $J_0(c)=c$ and, for $a\in T_d$, define $Q_S(a):=\omega_S(\Theta a\,a)$. Fix a finite positive-time polynomial $a=\sum_{j=0}^{N}a_j$, with each $a_j$ a finite sum of degree-$j$ product tests. Expanding concatenation and the moment functional gives the finite sum $Q_{S^\lambda}(a)=\sum_{j,k=0}^{N}\langle S^\lambda_{j+k},J_{j+k}((\Theta a_j)a_k)\rangle .$ Every test in this finite sum is fixed independently of $\lambda$, so [A2] gives $Q_{S^\lambda}(a)\to Q_S(a)$. By [A1], every value $Q_{S^\lambda}(a)$ is a nonnegative real number. Since $[0,\infty)$ is closed in $\mathbb C$, its limit $Q_S(a)$ is also a nonnegative real number. As $a$ was arbitrary, $S$ is reflection positive. [A1, A2, F1, given, algebra]

By [F3], the bounded linear isometry $\Omega_+$ has a bounded Hilbert
adjoint. For any $z$ in a Hilbert space,
$\|z\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|(z,x)|$: Cauchy–Schwarz gives the upper bound, and
if $z\ne0$ the choice $x=z/\|z\|$ attains it. For $y\in\mathcal H$, the
adjoint identity and [F2] therefore give
$\|\Omega_+^*y\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|(\Omega_+^*y,x)|
=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|(y,\Omega_+x)|\le\|y\|$, since $\|\Omega_+x\|=\|x\|$.
Therefore
$\|Sx\|=\|\Omega_+^*\Omega_-x\|\le\|\Omega_-x\|=\|x\|$ for every
$x\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{as}}$, so $S$ is a contraction.
[F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

actual_current_steps.1.2:
By [F3], the bounded maps $\Omega_\pm$ and $S$ have bounded Hilbert
adjoints with the stated adjoint identities. For either isometry $\Omega$,
the adjoint identity gives
$(x,\Omega^*\Omega y)=(\Omega x,\Omega y)=(x,y)$ for all $x,y$; nondegeneracy
therefore gives $\Omega^*\Omega=I$. For $P=\Omega\Omega^*$ the same identity
gives $(Px,y)=(\Omega^*x,\Omega^*y)=(x,Py)$, so $P^*=P$, and
$\Omega^*\Omega=I$ gives $P^2=P$. Also $P$ fixes each $\Omega x$ and its
image is contained in $\operatorname{Ran}\Omega$, so $P$ is the orthogonal
projection onto the closed range. If
$\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_+=\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_-=:R$, both products
are the same projection $P_R$. For all $x,z\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{as}}$,
$(Sx,z)_{\mathrm{as}}=(\Omega_-x,\Omega_+z)_{\mathcal H}
=(x,\Omega_-^*\Omega_+z)_{\mathrm{as}}$, so uniqueness of the adjoint gives
$S^*=\Omega_-^*\Omega_+$. It follows that
$S^*S=\Omega_-^*P_R\Omega_-=\Omega_-^*\Omega_-=I$ and
$SS^*=\Omega_+^*P_R\Omega_+=\Omega_+^*\Omega_+=I$, so $S$ is unitary.
[F1, F3, given, algebra]
actual_current_steps.2.1:
Conversely, suppose $S$ is unitary and put
$P_+=\Omega_+\Omega_+^*$. By [F3] and step 1.2 this is a bounded
orthogonal projection.
For each $x$,
$\|P_+\Omega_-x\|=\|\Omega_+^*\Omega_-x\|=\|Sx\|=\|x\|
=\|\Omega_-x\|$. For an orthogonal projection $P$, the identity
$\|Py\|=\|y\|$ implies
$\|y\|^2=\|Py\|^2+\|(I-P)y\|^2$ and hence $(I-P)y=0$; therefore
$\Omega_-x\in\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_+$ for every $x$, proving
$\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_-\subseteq\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_+$. Since $S$
is onto, for every $z\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{as}}$ choose $x$ with $Sx=z$.
Then $\Omega_+z=\Omega_+Sx=P_+\Omega_-x=\Omega_-x$, which gives the reverse
range inclusion. Thus the ranges coincide. [F1, F3, given, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

actual_current_steps.1.1: Fix $n\geq2$ and a tuple $(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n)$, and let $H$ be the simple graph on $[n]$ whose edge $\{i,j\}$ is present exactly when $\gamma_i\sim\gamma_j$. By [F1], $U_n=\sum_{G\subseteq H,\ G\text{ connected}}(-1)^{|E(G)|}$. Here the complete graph on $[n]$ has edge set $\binom{[n]}2$, and $G\subseteq H$ means that $G$ has the same vertex set and $E(G)\subseteq E(H)$. Represent each edge $\{i,j\}$ with $i<j$ by $(i,j)$ and order these pairs lexicographically, first by $i$ and then by $j$; list the edges as $e_1<_{\rm lex}\cdots<_{\rm lex}e_m$ and assign rank $\rho(e_k)=k\cdot1_{\mathbb R}$. For a tree $T$, its rank sum is $\sum_{e\in E(T)}\rho(e)$. By [F8], each connected graph $G$ has a spanning tree; by [F9], its spanning trees form a finite nonempty set, so their finite real rank sums have a minimum. A tree has a unique path between any two vertices: connectedness gives a path, and two distinct paths would contain a cycle between their first divergence and next common vertex, contradicting acyclicity. Here is the cut and exchange argument used below. Let $f=\{u,v\}$ be an edge of a tree $T$. There is no $u$-$v$ path in $T-f$, since such a path together with $f$ would be a cycle in $T$. For any vertex $w$, the unique $T$-path from $u$ to $w$ either avoids $f$, or crosses $f$ from $u$ to $v$ and then has a suffix from $v$ to $w$ avoiding $f$. Thus every vertex is reachable from $u$ or from $v$ in $T-f$, but not both: reachability from both would concatenate to a $u$-$v$ walk avoiding $f$, and deleting repeated-vertex portions of a finite walk gives a path, contradicting the preceding observation. Vertices reachable from the same endpoint are joined by concatenating their endpoint paths and deleting repetitions. Hence $T-f$ has exactly two connected components, with vertex sets $C_u,C_v$, and no remaining tree edge crosses this partition; call it the cut of $f$. If $e=\{x,y\}\notin E(T)$ and $f$ lies on its unique $T$-path, then $x,y$ lie in opposite components, for otherwise a path in $T-f$ would contradict uniqueness of the $T$-path. Adding $e$ to $T-f$ joins the two components, so $T-f+e$ is connected. It is acyclic: a cycle would have to use $e$ since $T-f$ is acyclic, and removing $e$ from that cycle would give a path in $T-f$ between opposite components. Thus $T-f+e$ is a spanning tree on the same vertex set. Every path from one side of any such cut to the other has a crossing edge, by considering the first vertex at which its finite vertex list changes sides. The minimum-rank-sum spanning tree is unique: if distinct minimizing trees $T,S$ existed, take the least-ranked edge $e$ in their symmetric difference and, after swapping their names if needed, take $e\in T\setminus S$. Deleting $e$ from $T$ gives a cut crossed by the $S$-path between the endpoints of $e$; a crossing edge $f$ on that path lies in $S\setminus T$, and replacing $f$ by the earlier edge $e$ lowers the rank sum of $S$ by [F10], a contradiction. For a tree $T$, let $A(T)\subseteq\binom{[n]}2\setminus E(T)$ consist of the edges later than every edge on their unique $T$-path. If $G$ contains $T$ and a non-tree edge $e$ is earlier than a path edge $f$, then $T-f+e$ is a spanning tree of lower rank sum by [F10], so $T$ is not minimum. Conversely, if every non-tree edge of $G$ is later than every edge on its $T$-path, then for each $f\in T$ every other edge of $G$ crossing the cut made by deleting $f$ is later than $f$. Choose a minimum-rank-sum spanning tree $S$ of $G$, which exists by [F8]–[F9]. If $S$ omitted $f$, the $S$-path between the endpoints of $f$ crosses this cut at an edge $e$; adding $f$ to $S$ and deleting that path edge $e$ gives a spanning tree with lower rank sum by [F10], contradicting minimality of $S$. Hence $S$ contains every edge $f$ of $T$ and equals $T$: any additional edge would form a cycle with its $T$-path. Thus $T$ is the unique minimum tree of $G$ exactly when $T\subseteq G\subseteq T\cup A(T)$. Consequently, connected subgraphs of $H$ split into disjoint classes indexed by trees $T\subseteq H$, each class consisting of $T\cup A$ for $A\subseteq A(T)\cap E(H)$. The signed sum in one class is $(-1)^{n-1}(1-1)^{|A(T)\cap E(H)|}$, whose real absolute value is at most $1$. Applying the finite-sum triangle inequality from [F5, F7] to the class contributions gives $|U_n(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n)|\leq\sum_{T\in\mathcal T_n}\prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}\mathbf 1_{\{\gamma_i\sim\gamma_j\}}$. For $n=1$ both sides equal $1$. [F1, F5, F7, F8, F9, F10, algebra]

actual_current_steps.1.1: Define the linear functional $\varphi(X):=\operatorname{tr}(\ell X)$ and the rank-one map $P(X):=\rho\,\varphi(X)$. Since $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$, $\rho\ne0$; the pairing normalization $\varphi(\rho)=1$ gives $P^2=P$. The fixed-point equations give $\mathcal EP=P$ and $P\mathcal E=P$, since $\varphi(\mathcal E(X))=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal E^*(\ell)X)=\varphi(X)$. Hence $M_D(\mathbb C)=\mathbb C\rho\oplus\ker\varphi$ is an $\mathcal E$-invariant direct sum, $\mathcal E$ is the identity on $\mathbb C\rho$, and $P$ is zero on $\ker\varphi$. If the restriction of $\mathcal E$ to $\ker\varphi$ had eigenvalue $1$, it would have a nonzero eigenvector $X$ there. Since $\varphi(X)=0$ and $\varphi(\rho)=1$, $X$ and $\rho$ would be linearly independent eigenvectors of $\mathcal E$ for $1$, so $\dim E_1(\mathcal E)\ge2$. But [F7]–[F8] identify the Statement's simple-root hypothesis with algebraic multiplicity one, and [F9] bounds this geometric multiplicity by the algebraic multiplicity. This contradiction shows that the restriction has no eigenvalue $1$. Therefore $\mathcal E^g-P$ is zero on $\mathbb C\rho$ and equals $(\mathcal E|_{\ker\varphi})^g$ on the invariant complement. Use $\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}:=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Xv\|$ on $M_D(\mathbb C)$ and the induced norm $\|\Phi\|:=\sup_{\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}=1}\|\Phi(X)\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ on its linear maps.
If $\ker\varphi=\{0\}$, then $\mathcal E=P=I$ and $\mathcal E^g-P=0$ for every $g\ge0$; for every allowed $r$, take $K_r=0$.
Otherwise the restriction is a finite-dimensional complex endomorphism of positive dimension $m$. Its characteristic polynomial is monic of degree $m$ by [F7]. By [F4] it has a root $\mu$. Write this characteristic polynomial as $p(x)=\sum_{k=0}^m c_kx^k$. Since $p(\mu)=0$, the identities $x^k-\mu^k=(x-\mu)\sum_{t=0}^{k-1}x^{k-1-t}\mu^t$ give $p(x)=(x-\mu)h(x)$ with $\deg h=m-1$. Induction on degree therefore shows that this characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors over $\mathbb C$. Now [F5] gives a similarity to finitely many Jordan blocks $J_s(\lambda)=\lambda I+N$ with $N^s=0$. Every such $\lambda$ belongs to $\sigma_{\mathbb C}(\mathcal E)\setminus\{1\}$, since an eigenvector of the restriction is also an eigenvector of $\mathcal E$ and step 1.1 excludes $1$ from the restricted spectrum; hence $|\lambda|\le q$.
If $q=0$, all Jordan powers of the restriction vanish for sufficiently large $g$, so $\mathcal E^g-P=0$ for those $g$. Since every allowed $r>q=0$ is positive, the finitely many remaining quantities $\|\mathcal E^g-P\|r^{-g}$ have a finite maximum; take this maximum as $K_r$ to obtain the required bound for all $g$.
If $q>0$, fix $r>q$. For a block with $\lambda\ne0$ and $g\ge s$, the binomial expansion gives $J_s(\lambda)^g=\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}\binom gj\lambda^{g-j}N^j$. For every fixed $j$, $g^j(|\lambda|/r)^g$ is bounded because the ratio of consecutive terms tends to $|\lambda|/r<1$; hence each matrix entry is bounded by a constant times $r^g$. Blocks with $\lambda=0$ vanish for $g\ge s$, and all finitely many smaller $g$ are absorbed into the constant. In the maximum-coordinate norm of the Jordan basis, the norm of the block-diagonal power is bounded by a constant times $r^g$, since there are finitely many blocks and each has finitely many entries; the zero action of $\mathcal E^g-P$ on $\mathbb C\rho$ adds only a one-dimensional zero block. The fixed change-of-basis map and its inverse have finite induced norms, so submultiplicativity transfers this bound to the stated superoperator norm: $\|\mathcal E^g-P\|\le K_r r^g$ for a finite $K_r$ and every $g\ge0$. [F3, F4, F5, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

Apply the defining integration-by-parts construction of the canonical
local representative to the term in step 2.1. The product rule gives
$$2\mathbf E_R^{bcd}\nabla_d\nabla_b\zeta_c =2\nabla_d(\mathbf E_R^{bcd}\nabla_b\zeta_c) -2(\nabla_d\mathbf E_R^{bcd})\nabla_b\zeta_c.$$
In form components, the second-derivative part of
$(d(X^{cd}\nabla_{[c}\zeta_{d]}))_{a_2\ldots a_n}$ is
$$-(n-1)P^{pqcd}(\boldsymbol\epsilon_g)_{pq[a_3\ldots a_n} \nabla_{a_2]}\nabla_{[c}\zeta_{d]}.$$
Antisymmetrizing $p,q$, $c,d$, and the form slots, then exchanging the
curvature-derivative index pairs of $P$, gives
$$2P^{abcd}(\boldsymbol\epsilon_g)_{a a_2\ldots a_n} \nabla_d\nabla_b\zeta_c,$$
which is the second-derivative term in step 2.1. Thus the coefficient and
sign of $X$ are fixed as stated. The remaining
terms in the product rule, the curvature commutator, and the other terms of
$J_\zeta$ contain at most first derivatives of $\zeta$. Repeatedly apply
$$A^a{}_b\nabla_a\zeta^b=\nabla_a(A^a{}_b\zeta^b) -(\nabla_aA^a{}_b)\zeta^b$$
to the lower-order terms in the canonical construction. Each step lowers
the derivative order on $\zeta$ by one, so the residual potential term is
linear in $\zeta$, denoted $W^c\zeta_c$. This proves the canonical formula.
The stipulated Lagrangian and potential changes contribute respectively
$\iota_\zeta\mu$ and $\mathbf Y(\phi;\mathcal L_\zeta\phi)$ to the charge;
an exact charge change contributes $dZ$. This gives the full stated class.

mapping.current_paragraph: Under $e^{-i\omega t}$ time dependence, $V_t$ has amplitude $-i\omega v$, so $(\gamma-i\omega)v=ae$. The scalar $\gamma-i\omega$ is nonzero because its imaginary part is $-\omega\ne0$; hence the vector equation gives $v=\bigl(a/(\gamma-i\omega)\bigr)e$, including when $e=0$. The conductivity is the scalar multiplier $\sigma(\omega):=a/(\gamma-i\omega)$ of this linear map. Multiplying numerator and denominator by $\gamma+i\omega$ gives $\operatorname{Re}\sigma=a\gamma/(\gamma^2+\omega^2)\ge0$. [given, A1, algebra]

mapping.current_paragraph: Dipole moment identities. The compact-ball verification in the preceding transverse-radiation theorem [F1] applies to the same $a>0$ and Countable Choice hypothesis: $\overline B_a$ is closed and bounded, hence compact; it is Borel and Lebesgue measurable; and $\lambda_3(\overline B_a)\le\lambda_3(B_{2a})<\infty$. Thus it is an admissible fixed integration set for [F3]. For each $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ put $p_i(u)=\int_{B_a}y_i\rho(y,u)\,dy$. Smoothness and vanishing of $\rho,J$ for $|y|>a$ imply that $\rho$, $J_i$ and their time derivatives vanish on $\partial B_a$. Thus the integrals of $y_i\rho$ and $y_i\rho_t$ over $B_a$ agree with those over that compact measurable finite-measure set $\overline B_a$. Apply the set form of [F3] with integration set $\overline B_a$ and parameter $u$ to $f_i(y,u)=y_i\rho(y,u)$; its parameter derivative is $y_i\rho_t(y,u)$, and both are continuous on a neighborhood of $\overline B_a$ times any compact time interval. This gives $p_i'(u)=\int_{B_a}y_i\rho_t(y,u)\,dy$. Fix $R_0>a$ and apply the divergence theorem to $y\mapsto y_iJ(y,u)$ on $B_{R_0}$. The boundary flux is zero because $J=0$ near $\partial B_{R_0}$, while $\operatorname{div}(y_iJ)=J_i+y_i\operatorname{div}J$. Using $\rho_t=-\operatorname{div}J$ and the vanishing of the source outside $B_a$ gives $p_i'(u)=\int_{B_a}J_i(y,u)\,dy$. For each $i$, the integrals of $J_i$ and $J_{i,t}$ over $B_a$ agree with those over $\overline B_a$; the closed ball has the compactness, measurability and finite measure just verified using [F1]. Both integrands are continuous on a neighborhood of $\overline B_a$ times any compact time interval. Apply the set form of [F3] on $\overline B_a$ separately to each component $J_i$ with parameter $u$; differentiating the preceding identity gives $p_i''(u)=\int_{B_a}J_{i,t}(y,u)\,dy$. Collecting the three component identities yields $p''(u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u)\,dy$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, A1]

mapping.current_paragraph:
In a local sphere chart with angular metric components $\gamma_{AB}$, the ingoing $(v,r)$ metric block and its inverse are
$$\begin{pmatrix}-D&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&D\end{pmatrix}.$$
The first block has determinant $-1$, so the full metric density is $w=r^2\sqrt{\det(\gamma_{AB})}$. Put $J^a:=g^{ab}\partial_b\widetilde\psi$. The spherical lift gives $J^v=\psi_r$, $J^r=\psi_v+D\psi_r$, and $J^A=0$; this vector field is $C^2$, so [F2] applies. By [F1], [F3] and metric compatibility, $\Box_g\widetilde\psi=\nabla_aJ^a$. Applying the density formula and cancelling the angular density, which is independent of $v,r$, gives
$$0=\Box_g\widetilde\psi=\frac1{r^2}\left[\partial_v(r^2\psi_r)+\partial_r\!\left(r^2(\psi_v+D\psi_r)\right)\right].$$
Expanding the derivatives and using equality of the continuous mixed partials yields
$$2r^2\psi_{vr}+2r\psi_v+\partial_r(r^2D\psi_r)=0.$$
[given, F1, F2, F3, A1, algebra]

Put $A=r^2+a^2$. In the ingoing chart the inverse metric has $g^{vr}=A/\Sigma$, $g^{\widetilde\phi r}=a/\Sigma$, and $g^{rr}=\Delta/\Sigma$. Thus on $H^+$, $\sharp_g(dr)=(A/\Sigma)\partial_v+(a/\Sigma)\partial_{\widetilde\phi}$ by [F9]. The stationary and axial fields remain $\partial_v$ and $\partial_{\widetilde\phi}$, so $\sharp_g(dr)=(A/\Sigma)(T+(a/A)\Phi)$. It follows that the null normal direction is $\chi=T+\Omega_H\Phi$ with $\Omega_H=a/(r_+^2+a^2)$. Equivalently, $\Delta(r_+)=0$ gives $2Mr_+=r_+^2+a^2$, and direct substitution yields $g(\chi,\chi)|_{r_+}=0$. The time orientation also extends explicitly. Write $R:=\partial_r$ in the ingoing product coordinates and set $\overline N:=T-(2Mr/\Sigma)R$. Step 2.1 gives $g(T,R)=1$, $g(R,R)=0$, and $g(T,T)=-(\Delta-a^2q)/\Sigma$. Since $\Sigma=r^2+a^2(1-q)$,
$$g(\overline N,\overline N)=-\frac{\Delta-a^2q+4Mr}{\Sigma}=-\frac{\Sigma+2Mr}{\Sigma}<0$$
on the entire extension, where $r>r_+-\varepsilon>0$. Both product coordinate fields and $\Sigma$ are smooth globally, including the rotation axis, so this is a smooth nowhere-zero timelike field there. On the exterior overlap, $t=v-f(r)$ and $f'=(r^2+a^2)/\Delta$ from step 2.1 imply
$$dt(\overline N)=1+\frac{2Mr(r^2+a^2)}{\Sigma\Delta}>0.$$
Thus $g(N,\overline N)=-dt(\overline N)<0$ by [F2], so the two timelike fields select the same future cone on the overlap. Finally put $A_+:=r_+^2+a^2$ and $\Sigma_+:=r_+^2+a^2(1-q)$. On $H^+$,
$$g(\chi,R)=1-a\Omega_Hq=\frac{\Sigma_+}{A_+}>0.$$
Since $\chi$ is normal to $H^+$ and $T$ is tangent, $g(\chi,T)=0$ there; using $2Mr_+=A_+$ gives
$$g(\chi,\overline N)=-\frac{A_+}{\Sigma_+}\frac{\Sigma_+}{A_+}=-1<0.$$
Therefore the nonzero null generator $\chi$ is future-directed in this proved compatible time orientation, without an extra orientation hypothesis. [A1, F1, F2, F5, F9, step 2.1, algebra]

Choose $0<\varepsilon<r_+/2$ and use the extension manifold $\overline{\mathcal M}:=\mathbb R_v\times(r_+-\varepsilon,\infty)\times S^2$ with its product smooth structure. Let $\bar\pi:\overline{\mathcal M}\to S^2$ be the sphere projection, $\bar\gamma:=\bar\pi^*\gamma_{S^2}$, $\eta:=\bar\pi^*(\gamma_{S^2}(\xi,\cdot))$, and $q:=\bar\gamma(\xi,\xi)=|\xi|_{\bar\gamma}^2$. These are global smooth tensors or functions; on a polar chart of the new sphere factor, $\eta=\sin^2\theta\,d\widetilde\phi$ and $q=\sin^2\theta$. Fix $r_0>r_+$ and define $f(r)=\int_{r_0}^r (s^2+a^2)/\Delta(s)\,ds$ and $h(r)=\int_{r_0}^r a/\Delta(s)\,ds$ on $(r_+,\infty)$. Their integrands are smooth because $\Delta>0$: repeated use of [F7] gives all derivatives of $\Delta^{-1}$, and [F8] handles the polynomial products. [F6] gives $f,h\in C^1$, and successive differentiation of $f'=(r^2+a^2)/\Delta$ and $h'=a/\Delta$ shows that both primitives are smooth. Set $v=t+f(r)$ and, on the sphere factor, replace each point $(x,y,z)$ by $R_{h(r)}(x,y,z):=(x\cos h-y\sin h,x\sin h+y\cos h,z)$. Repeated application of [F10] makes this rotation smoothly dependent on $r$, and its inverse is $R_{-h(r)}$. Thus the exterior map is a smooth diffeomorphism, with coordinate Jacobian determinant $1$ on every polar chart; there $\widetilde\phi=\phi+h(r)$ and the pullback of the original $\xi^\flat$ is $\eta-aq\Delta^{-1}dr$. Substitution in [F1], using $\Sigma^2+a^2q(\Sigma+2Mr)=(r^2+a^2)^2-a^2\Delta q$, gives the global ingoing expression
$$g=-\frac{\Delta-a^2q}{\Sigma}\,dv\otimes dv+dv\otimes dr+dr\otimes dv+\Sigma\bar\gamma+\frac{a^2(\Sigma+2Mr)}{\Sigma}\eta\otimes\eta-\frac{2aMr}{\Sigma}(dv\otimes\eta+\eta\otimes dv)-a(dr\otimes\eta+\eta\otimes dr).$$
For every $r>r_+-\varepsilon>r_+/2>0$, one has $\Sigma>0$ and $\Delta=A-2Mr<A$, where $A:=r^2+a^2$. If $\Delta\ge0$, then $A^2-a^2\Delta q\ge A^2-a^2\Delta\ge A^2-a^2A=Ar^2>0$; if $\Delta<0$, then $A^2-a^2\Delta q\ge A^2>0$. Consequently the angular restriction in an off-axis polar chart, $\Sigma\,d\theta^2+\frac{q(A^2-a^2\Delta q)}{\Sigma}\,d\widetilde\phi^2$, is positive definite. The determinant of the full metric matrix there is $-\Sigma^2q<0$; its Schur complement in the $(v,r)$ directions is symmetric with negative determinant, hence has one negative and one positive eigenvalue. The full metric therefore has signature $(-,+,+,+)$ off the axis. At an axis point $\eta=0$ and $\Sigma=A$; the $(v,r)$ block has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}-\Delta/\Sigma&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ of determinant $-1$, and the sphere block is $\Sigma\gamma_{S^2}$ on the tangent space, so the extension has the same Lorentzian signature there. Every coefficient in the global expression is smooth across $r=r_+$ because $\Sigma>0$ and no coefficient contains $\Delta$ in a denominator. It is a smooth Lorentzian extension across $r=r_+$. In this chart $g^{-1}(dr,dr)=\Delta/\Sigma$, so $dr(\sharp_gdr)=g^{-1}(dr,dr)=0$ on $H^+$ by [F9]; the normal is null and tangent there. [A1, F1, F2, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, algebra]

From [F1], $g(T,T)=-(1-2Mr/\Sigma)$. It is positive precisely when $r^2-2Mr+a^2\cos^2\theta<0$. The two roots of this quadratic in $r$ are $M\pm\sqrt{M^2-a^2\cos^2\theta}$; because $|a|<M$, they are real, and the upper root is $r_{\mathrm s}(\theta)$. The lower root is at most $r_-$, since $\cos^2\theta\le1$, and $r_-<r_+$; restricting the interval between the roots to the exterior therefore gives exactly $r_+<r<r_{\mathrm s}(\theta)$. At $\theta=0,\pi$ the upper root equals $r_+$. If $a\ne0$ and $0<\theta<\pi$, then $a^2\cos^2\theta<a^2$, so the upper root exceeds $r_+$; if $a=0$, the upper root equals $r_+$ for every $\theta$ and the ergoregion is empty. This proves the stated condition in all allowed cases. [F1, algebra] ∎

mapping.current_paragraph: If $Q,R\in SU(2)$, then $(QR)^\dagger QR=R^\dagger Q^\dagger QR=I_2$ and $\det(QR)=\det Q\det R=1$ by [F1]; $I_2$ is in the set. From $Q^\dagger Q=I_2$, the columns of $Q$ are linearly independent and hence $Q$ is invertible; therefore $Q^\dagger=Q^{-1}$ and $QQ^\dagger=I_2$. By [F1], $1=\det(I_2)=\det(QQ^\dagger)=\det Q\det(Q^\dagger)$, so $\det(Q^\dagger)=1$ and the inverse belongs to $SU(2)$. Associativity is inherited from matrix multiplication. The product entries are polynomials in real and imaginary entries and the inverse $Q\mapsto Q^\dagger$ is continuous, so these maps meet the topological-group definition [F4]. mapping.current_paragraph: Fix $x$ and set $f_x(y):=u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}$. The integrand $\widehat f_x$ is Schwartz and hence in $L^1$. Apply [F8] to the positive scaling $\eta\mapsto\xi=\epsilon\eta$, whose Jacobian is $\epsilon^d$, to obtain the substitution $\eta=\xi/\epsilon$ and $d\xi=\epsilon^d d\eta$. Write $\widehat f_x(\eta)=\int e^{-iy\cdot\eta}f_x(y)\,dy$, the rescaled negative-sign $2\pi$ transform. Then $$ \int W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,d\xi=(2\pi)^{-d}\int\widehat{f_x}(\eta)\,d\eta=f_x(0)=|u(x)|^2, $$ where the middle equality follows from [F4] at zero after the change from the library frequency $\eta/(2\pi)$ to $\eta$, also covered by [F8]. All integrals are absolutely convergent because $f_x,\widehat{f_x}\in\mathcal S$. [given, A1, F3, F4, F8, algebra]

For the momentum marginal, $u\in\mathcal S\subseteq L^1$, so the double integral in $x,y$ is absolutely integrable by Fubini [F5]. The affine change $(x,y)\mapsto(q,r)=(x+y/2,x-y/2)$ has absolute determinant $1$ and $q-r=y$; [F8] therefore gives $$ \int W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{-i(q-r)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(q)\overline{u(r)}\,dq\,dr=|(\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi)|^2. $$ The last equality is the product of the scaled Fourier integral with its complex conjugate. [given, A1, F2, F5, F8, algebra]

mapping.current_paragraph: The map $(x,y)\mapsto((x+y)/2,x-y)$ is an invertible linear map with absolute determinant $1$. The product of $a$, $u$, and $\overline u$ in the Weyl pairing is Schwartz in the transformed variables, so it is absolutely integrable. Fubini [F5] and change of variables [F8] give $$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,u\rangle=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a(q,\xi)u(q-r/2)\overline{u(q+r/2)}\,dq\,dr\,d\xi . $$ Applying [F8] to the reflection $y=-r$ turns the last two factors and the exponential into the defining integrand of $W_\epsilon[u]$; hence the pairing identity follows. [given, A1, F2, F5, F8, algebra]

mapping.current_paragraph: If $t=0$, then $\mathcal T_0=\operatorname{id}$ and $R(0)=I$; all positive-jump simplexes are empty, and the sole branch has weight $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. For $t>0$, applying the operator identity from step 3.1 to $\rho$ and expanding each occurrence of $\mathcal J$ in $S_n(t)$ sums over labels $a_1,\ldots,a_n$. Step 2.1 turns each factor $e^{u\mathcal N}$ into the no-jump conjugation, so each integrand is $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)\rho W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)^*$ by [F2]. This matrix is positive since $\langle W\rho W^*v,v\rangle=\langle\rho W^*v,W^*v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$; this argument uses only $\rho\geq0$, proving branch positivity for all positive inputs. All label sums at fixed $n$ are finite, and [F11] allows moving those sums and the finite-dimensional linear trace through the nested integrals. Trace-norm convergence from step 3.1 and the trace bound in [F5] then allow taking the trace of the infinite series. Each integrated branch weight is nonnegative: its continuous real trace integrand is pointwise nonnegative, and [F11] preserves this at every successive integration. For each vector $v$, the finite-dimensional linear functional $X\mapsto\langle Xv,v\rangle$ likewise commutes with these integrals by [F11]; its nonnegative integrand proves that every integrated branch state is positive. This positivity and convergence argument has not assumed the complete positivity of the final ensemble map. By [F6], $\operatorname{Tr}(e^{t\mathcal L}\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, so the nonnegative integrated branch weights sum to one. If $r=0$, then $\mathcal J=0$, all $S_n$ with $n\geq1$ vanish, and only the no-jump term remains. [F2, F4, F5, F6, F8, F11, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

Step 2.1 turns each factor $e^{u\mathcal N}$ into the no-jump conjugation, so each integrand is $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)\rho W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)^*$ by [F2]. mapping.current_paragraph: On $M_d(\mathbb C)$ define $\mathcal N(X)=KX+XK^*$, $\mathcal J(X)=\sum_aL_aXL_a^*$, and $\mathcal T_u=e^{u\mathcal L}$. By [F5], these finite sums of left and right matrix multiplications are bounded in trace norm. Expanding [F1] gives $\mathcal L=\mathcal N+\mathcal J$. Fix $t>0$. Integrate finite-dimensional matrix and superoperator entries by their real and imaginary components, using the repeated Riemann convention in [F2]. The curve $s\mapsto e^{(t-s)\mathcal N}\mathcal T_s$ has continuously differentiable entries by [F4]; its real and imaginary derivative components are continuous and hence integrable by [F8]. Differentiation gives $\frac{d}{ds}(e^{(t-s)\mathcal N}\mathcal T_s)=e^{(t-s)\mathcal N}\mathcal J\mathcal T_s$, since $\mathcal L=\mathcal N+\mathcal J$. Applying [F9] entrywise yields $\mathcal T_t=e^{t\mathcal N}+\int_0^t e^{(t-s)\mathcal N}\mathcal J\mathcal T_s\,ds$. This finite identity follows by induction on $N$: the base case is the displayed variation-of-constants identity, and substituting that identity for the final $\mathcal T_{s_1}$ in the remainder adds the next ordered-simplex term and a remainder with one more innermost time. Only finite linearity of the nested integrals is used; no integration order is exchanged. Thus, for each $N\geq0$, $\mathcal T_t=\sum_{n=0}^{N}S_n(t)+Q_{N+1}(t)$, where $S_0(t)=e^{t\mathcal N}$, $S_n(t)=\int_{0<s_1<\cdots<s_n<t}e^{(t-s_n)\mathcal N}\mathcal J e^{(s_n-s_{n-1})\mathcal N}\cdots\mathcal J e^{s_1\mathcal N}\,d\mathbf s$ for $n\geq1$, and $Q_m(t)=\int_{0<s_1<\cdots<s_m<t}e^{(t-s_m)\mathcal N}\mathcal J\bigl(\prod_{j=m-1,\ldots,1}e^{(s_{j+1}-s_j)\mathcal N}\mathcal J\bigr)\mathcal T_{s_1}\,d\mathbf s$ for $m=N+1$, where the product is ordered from left to right with descending $j$, and the empty product is the identity. For $m=1$ the intermediate exponential factors are absent: $Q_1(t)=\int_0^t e^{(t-s_1)\mathcal N}\mathcal J\mathcal T_{s_1}\,ds_1$, exactly the displayed variation-of-constants remainder. In particular there is no extra $e^{s_1\mathcal N}$ before $\mathcal T_{s_1}$. All these integrands are continuous in finite-dimensional coordinates on the closed ordered simplex; [F11] proves that every inner integral is continuous in its remaining parameters and hence the full repeated integral exists. The insertion of one further nested integral in the induction is therefore legitimate. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F8, F9, F11, algebra]

mapping.current_paragraph:
Put $c=\hbar^2/(2m)$,
$M_n(k_y,k_z)=E_n+ck_z^2$, and
$\widehat M_n=M_n/E_{\mathrm{ref}}$. Apply [F1] to the three-dimensional
core form. The normalized closed form has coefficient multiplier
$\widehat M_n$; apply [F2] under the choice hypotheses in [A2]. For a
form-domain vector $F$, its representing operator domain consists exactly
of those $F$ for which there is $G\in L^2$ with
$$\sum_n\int \widehat M_nF_n\overline{H_n}=\sum_n\int G_n\overline{H_n}$$
for every form-domain $H$. If such $G$ exists, fix $n$ and any bounded box
$K\subset\mathbb R^2$. Since $\widehat M_n$ is bounded on $K$, both
$1_K\widehat M_nF_n$ and $1_KG_n$ are in $L^2(K)$. Choose the test vector
with sole component $H_n=1_K(\widehat M_nF_n-G_n)$; it belongs to the form
domain because its index and support are bounded. The identity forces
$$\int_K|\widehat M_nF_n-G_n|^2=0.$$
Exhausting $\mathbb R^2$ by bounded boxes and all $n$ gives
$G_n=\widehat M_nF_n$ almost everywhere, so $\widehat MF\in L^2$.
Conversely, if $\widehat MF\in L^2$, then for every form-domain $H$,
Cauchy–Schwarz gives
$$\sum_n\int \widehat M_nF_n\overline{H_n}=\langle\widehat MF,H\rangle,$$
so [F2] represents the normalized operator by multiplication by
$\widehat M_n$, with domain $\sum_n\int \widehat M_n^2|F_n|^2<\infty$.
Since $E_{\mathrm{ref}}>0$, this is equivalent to
$\sum_n\int M_n^2|F_n|^2<\infty$. The physical Hamiltonian
$H=E_{\mathrm{ref}}\widehat H$ therefore acts by multiplication by $M_n$
on this same domain. This identification follows under [A2]. [A1, A2, F1, F2, construct, algebra]

For $h$ with $s+h$ in the interval, the group law gives $\frac{w(s+h)-w(s)}h=U(s+h)\frac{v(s+h)-v(s)}h+U(s)\frac{W(h/\hbar)-I}{h}v(s)$. By [F1], $U$ is strongly continuous and unitary, the first term tends to $U(s)v'(s)$, and since $v(s)\in D(T)$ the second tends to $\frac{i}{\hbar}U(s)Tv(s)$ by the derivative of $W$ at zero and the scalar chain rule. Thus $w$ is differentiable and $w'(s)=U(s)v'(s)+\frac{i}{\hbar}U(s)Tv(s)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}U(s)r(s)$, after substituting $i\hbar v'=Tv+r$. The derivative is continuous because $v'$, $Tv$, and hence $r$ are continuous and $U$ is strongly continuous. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

Thus the induced functional pullback preserves the local polynomial class and has inverse $C_{\rho^{-1}}^*$. The mass relabelling composes as $\tau^{-1}\rho^{-1}m=(\rho\tau)^{-1}m$, including $m=0$, so the functional action obeys $\sigma_{\rho\tau}=\sigma_\rho\sigma_\tau$ and $\sigma_{\rho^{-1}}$ is its inverse. The induced conjugations on map families obey the same composition law, because the pullbacks compose as $C_\rho^*C_\tau^*=C_{\rho\tau}^*$ and the mass labels reindex in that same order. For $T_a\phi(x)=\phi(x-a)$, direct substitution gives $C_\rho T_a C_\rho^{-1}=T_{\rho a}$; scalar dilations commute with each Lorentz transformation. By [F3] this action normalizes the proper orthochronous Poincare group, and by [F4] conjugation preserves covariance of the time-ordered system. [given, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

By [F1], the Axiom of Choice [A1] supplies the Countable Choice hypothesis of [F2]. For $\mathbf k\in M$,
$$\mathbf k\cdot U(R)f(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k\cdot Rf(R^{-1}\mathbf k)=(R^{-1}\mathbf k)\cdot f(R^{-1}\mathbf k)=0,$$
so $U(R)$ preserves transversality. Since $R$ preserves $d
u$ by [F2] and preserves the Hermitian norm on $\mathbb C^3$, change of variables gives $\|U(R)f\|_
u=\|f\|_
u$. The same formula with $R^{-1}$ is an inverse, so $U(R)$ is unitary. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

For a unit axis $\mathbf a$ and $f\in\mathcal D$, differentiating $R_{\mathbf a}(t)f(R_{\mathbf a}(-t)\mathbf k)$ at $t=0$ gives $(\mathbf a\times f)(\mathbf k)-(\mathbf a\times\mathbf k)\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf k}f(\mathbf k)$. Because $-iS_{\mathbf a}v=\mathbf a\times v$, this equals $-\frac{i}{\hbar}(L_{\mathbf a}+S_{\mathbf a}^{\mathrm{op}})f$. The support stays in a fixed annulus for $t$ near $0$; the composite is smooth on a compact time interval times that annulus, so [F4] makes its $t$-derivative uniformly continuous. The integral form of the difference quotient gives uniform convergence in $\mathbf k$, hence convergence in $L^2(d\nu)$ because the annulus has finite measure. Thus every $f\in\mathcal D$ lies in the domain of the Stone generator and the differential formula holds there. [given, F2, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

mapping.current_paragraph: Put $A=[\mathbf a]_\times$, so $A^T=-A$. The norm-convergent power series for the matrix exponential gives continuity in $t$, $R_{\mathbf a}(s+t)=R_{\mathbf a}(s)R_{\mathbf a}(t)$, and $R_{\mathbf a}(t)^T=R_{\mathbf a}(-t)$; hence $R_{\mathbf a}(t)$ is orthogonal. Its determinant is continuous, takes values in $\{+1,-1\}$, and equals $1$ at $t=0$, so it is $1$ for all $t$ and $R_{\mathbf a}(t)\in SO(3)$. Therefore $t\mapsto U(R_{\mathbf a}(t))$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group by steps 1.1, 2.1, and 2.2. Applying Stone's theorem [F3] gives its unique self-adjoint generator $T_{\mathbf a}$ with $U(R_{\mathbf a}(t))=e^{itT_{\mathbf a}}$. Set $J_{\mathbf a}=-\hbar T_{\mathbf a}$; it is self-adjoint and satisfies $U(R_{\mathbf a}(t))=e^{-itJ_{\mathbf a}/\hbar}$. The derivative characterization in [F3] and step 3.1 give $J_{\mathbf a}=L_{\mathbf a}+S_{\mathbf a}^{\mathrm{op}}$ on $\mathcal D$. This uses Stone's self-adjoint generator and makes no essential-self-adjointness claim about the restricted differential expression. [A1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

mapping.current_paragraph: Restricting the labels and vertex gauge transformations to a boundary transports each attaching word and its flatness equation, so the resulting edge assignment is still flat. If a boundary identification reverses a chosen edge direction, the transported label is inverted, and $(h_{t(e)}g_eh_{s(e)}^{-1})^{-1}=h_{s(e)}g_e^{-1}h_{t(e)}^{-1}$ is exactly the gauge action on that reversed edge. Thus the reindexed restrictions $r_0,r_1$ are functors. Pullback and homotopy-fiber pushforward therefore define $Z_M$ by [F2]; both are linear because they are substitution and finite weighted summation. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

mapping.current_paragraph: Stability at $N=2$ gives $v(x)\geq-2B$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$; hence $-1\leq f_\beta(x)\leq e^{2\beta B}-1$ by [F12]. Thus for each fixed $N$ every graph term in the finite expansion $\prod_{i<j}(1+f_\beta(x_i-x_j))$ is bounded and measurable on the finite-measure box $\Lambda_L^N$. Expanding the product gives a sum over all simple graphs; each graph decomposes uniquely into connected components as in [F2]. If the component sizes are $m_1,\ldots,m_k$, assigning the $N$ labels to an ordered list of blocks contributes $N!/\prod_jm_j!$, and division by $k!$ removes block order. Integrating a product over disjoint coordinate blocks factorizes by Fubini [F5], since the factors are bounded on finite-measure boxes. Therefore the coefficient of $z^N$ in $\Xi_L$ equals that in the formal exponential of $A_L(z):=\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{z^n}{n!}\int_{\Lambda_L^n}U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n$. [A1, F1, F2, F5, F11, F12, F17, F23, given, algebra]

mapping.current_paragraph: For $n\geq2$, integrate the pointwise tree estimate [F2] over $\Lambda_L^n$. Root each tree at vertex $1$, then remove leaves other than the root. At each removal the leaf integral over $\Lambda_L$ is at most the whole-space integral $C_\beta$ by monotonicity [F19] and translation invariance [F6]; Tonelli [F10] applies to the nonnegative tree products. The final root integral is $|\Lambda_L|$. The labelled-tree count in [F2] is $n^{n-2}$. Finite additivity [F20] sums those tree integrals, giving $\int_{\Lambda_L^n}|U_n|\leq e^{2\beta Bn}|\Lambda_L|n^{n-2}C_\beta^{n-1}$. Thus $U_n$ is integrable on $\Lambda_L^n$. Regard its real values as complex values by the real embedding; [F21] identifies the complex modulus with real absolute value, so the integral triangle inequality [F18] gives $|b_n(L)|\leq e^{2\beta Bn}n^{n-2}C_\beta^{n-1}/n!$. mapping.current_paragraph: If $\pi_\theta=\pi_\varphi$ as functions on $X$, positivity allows taking logarithms of their equal positive values. The product law and inverse identity [F5, F6] then give $(\theta-\varphi)\cdot T(x)=A(\theta)-A(\varphi)$ for every $x$. Under minimality this forces $\theta-\varphi=0$. Conversely, if a nonzero $a$ makes $a\cdot T(x)=c$ constant, the exponential addition formula [F7] gives $Z(\theta+ta)=\exp(tc)Z(\theta)$. Since $Z(\theta)>0$ and $\exp(tc)>0$ by [F1, F8], the logarithm laws [F5, F6] give $A(\theta+ta)=A(\theta)+tc$. Substitution in the family formula and another use of [F7] show $\pi_{\theta+ta}=\pi_\theta$ for every real $t$; the parametrization is not injective. [F1, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

mapping.current_paragraph: Put $C=c_H$ and $T=\overline S$. The definition of graph closure above makes $A:=\widetilde T$ a closed densely defined complex-linear operator $\overline H\to H$. By [F2], write $A=U B$, where $B=(A^*A)^{1/2}$ is positive self-adjoint with $D(B)=D(A)$ and $U$ is a partial isometry with initial space $\overline{\operatorname{ran}B}=(\ker A)^\perp$, final space $\overline{\operatorname{ran}A}$, and kernel $\ker A$. Set $J:=UC$ and $P:=C^{-1}BC$, with domain $D(P)=C^{-1}D(B)$. The composition $P$ is linear. If $E$ is the spectral measure of $B$, then $F(\Lambda):=C^{-1}E(\Lambda)C$ is a spectral measure of orthogonal projections on $H$, and its spectral integral is $P$; hence $P$ is positive self-adjoint. More explicitly, $D(T^*T)=\{x:Cx\in D(A),\ ACx\in D(A^*)\}=C^{-1}D(A^*A)$, and the adjoint convention [F1] gives $T^*T=C^{-1}A^*AC$ there. Also $D(P^2)=C^{-1}D(B^2)$ and $P^2=C^{-1}B^2C=C^{-1}A^*AC=T^*T$ on that domain; uniqueness of the positive self-adjoint square root gives $P=(T^*T)^{1/2}$. For $x\in D(T)$, $JPx=UCC^{-1}BCx=UBCx=ACx=Tx$, so $T=JP$. The operator $J$ is antilinear, vanishes on $\ker T$, and is isometric on $(\ker T)^\perp$, since $C$ maps $\ker T$ onto $\ker A$ and preserves orthogonality. Its final space is $\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$. If $T$ is injective and has dense range, then $A$ is injective with dense range, so $U$ is unitary by [F2] and $J=UC$ is antiunitary. [A1, F1, F2, F5, construct, algebra]

mapping.current_paragraph:
By [F1], $S_N^z$ is diagonal in the tensor basis with eigenvalues
$-N/2,-N/2+1,\ldots,N/2$, so its weight spaces form an orthogonal direct
sum of $\mathcal H_N$. Since $[H_N,S_N^z]=0$ by step 2.1, each
$\mathcal H_{N,m}$ is invariant under $H_N$ and under every power $H_N^r$.
The series defining $\exp(-\beta H_N)$ converges in operator norm by [F4].
Its partial sums preserve every $\mathcal H_{N,m}$, and their
limits do as well because these subspaces are closed. The exponential is
therefore block diagonal for the orthogonal decomposition
$\mathcal H_N=\bigoplus_m\mathcal H_{N,m}$. In a basis formed by concatenating
orthonormal bases of the blocks, its matrix is block diagonal, so its trace
is the sum of the traces of the restrictions. Basis independence [F5] gives
the stated identity. [given, F1, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

For each $n\ge1$, let $J_n:[0,T]\to L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ take the value $J(kT/n)$ on $[kT/n,(k+1)T/n)$ for $0\le k<n$ and the value $J(T)$ at $T$. Each $J_n$ is a measurable simple function. Uniform continuity of $J$ on $[0,T]$ gives $\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|J_n(t)-J(t)\|_2\to0$, and hence $\int_0^T\|J_n(t)-J(t)\|_2\,dt\to0$. Thus $J$ is strongly measurable (an almost-everywhere limit of measurable simple functions), and $\int_0^T\|J(t)\|_2\,dt<\infty$ because $J$ is bounded. By the definition of the Bochner integral as the $L^1$-norm limit of integrals of simple functions, $J$ is Bochner integrable. The Bochner integrals of $J_n$ are the left-endpoint Riemann sums for $J$; they converge both to the Bochner integral by the $L^1$ approximation and to the norm-Riemann integral by [F6]. Hence these integrals agree. The expectation functional $\Lambda(Y):=\mathbb E[Y]=\langle Y,1\rangle_{L^2}$ is bounded since $|\Lambda(Y)|=|\langle Y,1\rangle_{L^2}|\le\|Y\|_2\|1\|_2=\|Y\|_2$. Applying the bounded-linear-map clause of [F6] gives $\mathbb E[X_T]=\int_0^T\mathbb E[J(t)]\,dt=0$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X_T)=\mathbb E[X_T^2]$. [given, F6, construct, algebra]

The spatially normalized current convention is fixed by [F1]. In the quantum alternative, [A1] and [F2] apply to the exact $\alpha_t$, invariant state $\phi$, and centered self-adjoint $V$ in the Statement, so the supplier gives the variance identity and limit. The evenness asserted in the Statement follows from $C(-t)=\operatorname{Re}\phi(V\alpha_{-t}(V))=\operatorname{Re}\phi(\alpha_t(V)V)=\operatorname{Re}\overline{\phi(V\alpha_t(V))}=C(t)$, using invariance and self-adjointness. In the classical alternative, continuity of the inner product makes $(s,t)\mapsto\mathbb E[J(s)J(t)]=C(t-s)$ continuous on $[0,T]^2$. Riemann sums for $X_T$ converge in $L^2$, so continuity of the inner product makes the expectations of their squared norms converge to $\mathbb E[X_T^2]$; each squared-sum expectation is a product Riemann sum for this continuous kernel. Thus [F3] gives $\mathbb E[X_T^2]=\int_0^T\int_0^T C(t-s)\,ds\,dt$, which equals $\operatorname{Var}(X_T)$ by step 1.1. The integrand is symmetric because $C$ is even. The diagonal has zero area: it lies in strips of width $\delta$ and area at most $2T\delta+\delta^2$, tending to zero, so a bounded continuous integrand contributes zero there. Off the diagonal the two triangular restrictions are continuous; on a grid meeting the diagonal their upper-lower gap is bounded by the kernel oscillation away from the diagonal plus twice its supremum times the diagonal-strip area. Hence the product of the triangular indicator with the kernel is Riemann integrable. Each section has at most one jump and is therefore Riemann integrable. For the upper triangle, $g(t):=\int_0^t C(t-s)\,ds$ satisfies $|g(t)-g(t\prime)|\le T\omega_C(|t-t\prime|)+\|C\|_\infty|t-t\prime|$, where $\omega_C(\delta):=\sup_{|u-v|\le\delta}|C(u)-C(v)|\to0$; hence its outer integral is continuous. The lower triangle has the same estimate with reversed limits. Splitting the square into its two triangles and applying [F3] to each gives $2\int_0^T\int_0^t C(t-s)\,ds\,dt$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

mapping.current_paragraph: Put $\tau=\chi u$, $\kappa=k/\chi$, $x_H=\chi U_H$, and $\lambda=Ak>0$. In the length coordinate $\tau$, the map $x(\tau):=\ell(\tau/\chi)$ satisfies $x(\tau)=x_H+\lambda U_\kappa(\tau)$, since $\lambda U_\kappa(\tau)=-\chi A e^{-\kappa\tau}$. By [F1], $U_\kappa$ is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism from $\mathbb R$ onto $(-\infty,0)$; the positive affine map $y\mapsto x_H+\lambda y$ is a smooth diffeomorphism from $(-\infty,0)$ onto $(-\infty,x_H)$. Since $u\mapsto\tau=\chi u$ is also a positive linear diffeomorphism, $\ell$ is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism from $\mathbb R$ onto $(-\infty,\ell_H)$, with smooth inverse $u_\ell(x)=\chi^{-1}U_\kappa^{-1}((x-x_H)/\lambda)$. Differentiating the supplied coordinate formula gives $\ell'(u)=\chi\lambda e^{-\kappa\chi u}=\chi Ak e^{-ku}$ and hence $U'(u)=Ak e^{-ku}>0$. If $\operatorname{supp}g\subseteq[a,b]$, then $\operatorname{supp}f_g\subseteq[\ell(a),\ell(b)]\subset(-\infty,\ell_H)$, so the zero extension is smooth and compactly supported. Thus $J(f_g)$ is defined by [F1]–[F2]. [given, A1, F1, F2, construct, algebra]
